t: Mini Parser — Deserialize a Nested List with Recursion or an Explicit Stack
o: We are given a string that serializes either a single integer (e.g. "324") or a nested list of integers/lists (e.g. "[123,[456,[789]]]"). We must rebuild the corresponding `NestedInteger` object tree. In example 1, the whole string is one number, so we return a NestedInteger holding 324. In example 2, the outer brackets form a list with two elements: integer 123, and a list containing 456 and another list containing 789 — nesting is arbitrary. Constraints allow up to 5*10^4 characters, so any linear-time parse works; there is no need for anything cleverer than a single left-to-right scan.
k: The input is a valid serialization, so parsing can be done in one linear pass without error handling.
Nesting depth maps naturally to recursion depth (DFS) or to stack depth (iterative simulation).
A number token may be multi-digit and negative; it ends at ',' or ']' or end of string.

a.i: Treat the string as a grammar: input := number | '[' list ']'. A recursive function parses starting at index i: if s[i] is '[', create a list NestedInteger and repeatedly parse elements separated by commas until the matching ']'; otherwise scan digits/sign to read one integer. Each '[' pushes one level of recursion, which exactly mirrors the nesting structure, so this is just a recursive-descent parser over a trivially simple grammar.
s: Maintain a global/current index i into s.
If s[i] == '[', advance i, create a new list NestedInteger; while s[i] != ']', recursively parse an element and add it, skipping ',' between elements; then consume ']' and return the list.
Otherwise scan characters while they are '-' or a digit to build the integer, return a NestedInteger wrapping it.
Call the parser once on the whole string and return the result.
a.t: O(n) — each character is consumed exactly once by the parser.
a.sp: O(d) recursion stack where d is maximum nesting depth (O(n) worst case like "[[[[...]]]]").

a.i: Replace recursion with an explicit stack of currently-open lists. On '[' push a fresh list; on ']' pop it and attach it to the new top (or make it the answer if the stack empties); on a complete number token add it to the top of the stack. This avoids Python/Java recursion-depth concerns and processes the string in one pass.
s: Initialize an empty stack and iterate over s with index i.
On '[': create a list NestedInteger and push it.
On ']': pop the top; if the stack is non-empty, add it to the new top, else it is the final answer.
On digit or '-': scan the full number token, wrap it in a NestedInteger, and add it to the stack top (if the stack is empty, the number itself is the answer).
a.t: O(n) — every character is examined once; number scanning advances i past whole tokens.
a.sp: O(d) explicit stack for d nesting levels, O(n) worst case.

w: In an interview, present the recursive DFS first since it directly mirrors the nested structure and is easiest to explain, then mention the iterative stack version as a robustness improvement against deep inputs (Python's default recursion limit ~1000 could be hit with 5*10^4 nested brackets). Pitfalls: forgetting negative numbers when scanning tokens, not advancing the index past ',' and ']', mishandling the bare-integer case "324" or "-5" where no brackets exist at all, and off-by-one errors around consuming the closing bracket. Edge cases to test: single integer, negative integers, empty-ish nesting like "[]"-style structures per problem guarantees, and deeply nested chains. Likely follow-ups: serialize the NestedInteger back to a string (LeetCode 394-style reverse), handle malformed input with validation, or stream-parse without random access.
